questions.question: What is algorithm efficiency?
options: The visual neatness of the block arrangement in the workspace
A measure of how well an algorithm uses time and memory resources as input size grows
The number of lines of code written to solve a problem
Whether an algorithm produces the correct output for a single test case
questions.explanation: Algorithm efficiency measures how an algorithm's time and space resource usage scales with increasing input size, independent of hardware.

questions.question: What is meant by best-case execution?
options: The scenario where the algorithm uses the most memory
The scenario where the algorithm takes the longest time to complete
The most favorable input arrangement that minimizes the algorithm's execution steps
The average number of steps taken across all possible inputs
questions.explanation: Best-case execution refers to the input that causes the algorithm to complete in the fewest possible steps — for example, finding a search target at the very first position.

questions.question: What is meant by worst-case execution?
options: The input that causes the algorithm to crash or fail
The most unfavorable input that causes the algorithm to take the maximum number of steps
The scenario with the highest memory allocation
Any input where the algorithm returns an incorrect result
questions.explanation: Worst-case execution is the upper bound on performance — the hardest possible input for the algorithm, such as searching for a target that doesn't exist in an array.

questions.question: What is Big-O notation?
options: A notation system for writing Python functions
A visual chart showing algorithm block counts
A mathematical notation that describes the upper bound of an algorithm's growth rate as input size approaches infinity
A grading scale for measuring code readability
questions.explanation: Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's resource usage grows in the worst case as n (input size) increases, abstracting away hardware and constant factors.

questions.question: Why does Big-O ignore hardware differences?
options: Because hardware is always the same across all computers
Because Big-O focuses on the mathematical growth rate of the algorithm itself, which is independent of the machine running it
Because hardware does not affect how fast code runs
Because Big-O only applies to programs running in the cloud
questions.explanation: Big-O strips away constant factors and hardware-specific speeds to focus purely on how the number of operations scales with n, making it a universal measure.

questions.question: What complexity class is O(log n)?
options: Quadratic — grows quadratically with input size
Linear — grows proportionally with input size
Constant — does not grow with input size
Logarithmic — grows very slowly, halving the problem at each step
questions.explanation: O(log n) is logarithmic complexity. Algorithms in this class typically cut the problem in half at each step, such as Binary Search.

questions.question: What complexity class is O(n²)?
options: Linear — grows proportionally to input size
Logarithmic — grows slowly
Quadratic — grows proportional to the square of the input size
Exponential — doubles with each additional input
questions.explanation: O(n²) is quadratic complexity, typically caused by nested loops where the outer and inner loops each iterate n times.

questions.question: Which is faster: O(1) or O(n)?
options: O(n), because it processes more elements
They are equal for all input sizes
O(1), because it executes in constant time regardless of input size
It depends entirely on the hardware being used
questions.explanation: O(1) is always faster in terms of growth rate because it never increases with n, while O(n) grows linearly as input size increases.

questions.question: Which is slower: O(n log n) or O(n²)?
options: O(n log n), because logarithms are slow
They are always equal
O(n²), because it grows much faster for large values of n
It cannot be determined without knowing the exact input
questions.explanation: O(n²) is significantly slower than O(n log n) for large inputs. For example, at n=1000, O(n²) = 1,000,000 operations vs O(n log n) ≈ 10,000.

questions.question: What does space complexity measure?
options: The physical disk space needed to install the program
The number of blocks in the workspace
The amount of memory (RAM) an algorithm uses as a function of input size
The time taken to allocate variables at program startup
questions.explanation: Space complexity measures how much memory an algorithm requires relative to its input size, including variables, data structures, and call stack frames.

questions.question: Does faster execution always result in lower memory usage?
options: Yes, faster algorithms always use less memory
No, there is often a time-space tradeoff where using more memory can speed up execution, and vice versa
Yes, because the CPU handles both time and memory the same way
No, but memory usage is always irrelevant to algorithm design
questions.explanation: There is a common time-space tradeoff: using additional memory (like a cache or lookup table) can dramatically reduce execution time, but at the cost of higher memory usage.

questions.question: How does array allocation affect space complexity?
options: It has no effect on space complexity
Allocating an array of size n adds O(n) to the space complexity
Arrays always use O(1) space regardless of their size
Array allocation only affects time complexity, not space
questions.explanation: Each element in an array requires memory, so allocating an array of size n contributes O(n) to the algorithm's space complexity.

questions.question: How does deep recursion affect space complexity?
options: It has no impact because recursion is handled by the CPU automatically
It reduces space complexity by reusing the same memory frame
Each recursive call adds a new stack frame, increasing space complexity proportional to the recursion depth
Deep recursion only affects time complexity, not space complexity
questions.explanation: Every recursive call creates a new stack frame on the call stack. For a recursion depth of n, this adds O(n) space complexity even if no other data structures are used.

questions.question: What is a computational bottleneck?
options: A syntax error that prevents the program from compiling
The part of an algorithm with the highest complexity that dominates overall performance
A hardware limitation that slows down all programs equally
A loop that executes exactly once
questions.explanation: A computational bottleneck is the section of code with the highest time or space complexity — it dominates the algorithm's overall Big-O rating and is the primary target for optimization.

questions.question: What defines algorithmic scalability?
options: Whether the algorithm can be rewritten in a different programming language
The number of programmers needed to maintain the algorithm
How well an algorithm maintains acceptable performance as input size increases significantly
Whether the algorithm uses loops or recursive functions
questions.explanation: Scalability refers to how an algorithm performs as n grows large. A scalable algorithm (e.g., O(n log n)) remains practical at large input sizes, while an unscalable one (e.g., O(2ⁿ)) becomes infeasible quickly.
